slides.title: The whole system must preserve one end-to-end contract
keyPoints: Every accepted byte contributes exactly once
Resources remain bounded under the stated scope
Threads finish before shared storage is destroyed
Parallel performance is measured, not assumed
slides.narration: The capstone combines byte representation, input extents, memory ownership, queue synchronization, worker lifetimes, and output verification. The sequential utility remains our reference. A concurrent result must match it even if the operating system runs all workers on one core in an interleaved order. The design does not promise speed merely because it uses threads. It promises that accepted bytes are counted once, partial results are combined correctly, and failures do not print a misleading successful total. We will follow ownership and publication boundaries before discussing throughput, because a faster pipeline with duplicated slots or dangling storage is not the same program.

slides.title: Partition seven items without dropping the remainder
keyPoints: Three workers receive ranges of lengths 2, 2, and 3
Each writes one separate result element
Joining precedes the ordered report
slides.narration: The earlier fixed six-item example splits evenly; this new fixture uses seven items and three workers. Integer boundary calculations give ranges zero through two, two through four, and four through seven, with the right endpoint excluded. Their lengths are two, two, and three, so no remainder is lost. Each jthread captures its worker index by value and writes only its own result slot. The vector of thread owners is destroyed before main reads those results, and jthread joins on destruction. The printed total is twenty-eight, equal to the sequential reference. No speed claim or scheduling-dependent output is made.

slides.title: Slot identity must have exactly one current owner
keyPoints: Free → producer → ready → worker → free
A duplicate return violates the ownership state
This model checks transitions without running a queue
slides.narration: This small state model gives two buffer slots a current owner. Slot zero moves from free to producer, then ready, then worker, then free again. Both slots are now free, so the first output is free slots equals two. A second attempted worker-to-free return fails because the slot is no longer worker-owned; duplicate rejected is one. The program does not implement queue synchronization. It isolates the invariant that the real queue transfers must preserve. Returning one slot twice could let two later users overwrite the same storage, while losing a slot could reduce capacity until progress stops.

slides.title: Choose arithmetic that permits the intended combination
keyPoints: Unsigned modular addition is associative
A byte contributes a value from 0 through 255
Byte-count overflow has a separate check
An additive checksum is not cryptographic authentication
slides.narration: The source pipeline treats input as uninterpreted bytes and adds their unsigned values into a sixty-four-bit sum. Unsigned modular addition can be regrouped, so worker partial sums can combine in any completion order under that arithmetic contract. A signed overflow or a strict floating-point reduction would need a different argument. The byte count is separately checked rather than assumed safe because the sum uses unsigned arithmetic. This simple checksum makes an integration lesson easier to verify, but does not authenticate input or resist deliberate collisions. Replacing it with an order-sensitive hash requires defining a correct parallel combination rule before reusing the worker structure.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
keyPoints: This fixed six-element teaching program does not handle arbitrary sizes, worker-start failure recovery, or cancellation. Those are explicit extension tasks, not implied guarantees.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Let workers push_back into the shared results vector without a lock, or let main return before collecting workers. The first can race on container internals; the second can leave dangling references.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Allocate the result slots before starting workers, assign each slot to one input, and keep all shared objects alive through worker completion. Preserve close-and-collect cleanup if any operation fails.

slides.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
keyPoints: Work items own their strings, so queue operations do not leave borrowed input pointers behind. Main assigns each index once; workers therefore write distinct result elements without resizing the vector. Queue predicates and close are protected by one mutex. Every normal and exceptional path closes the queue and collects workers before local shared state dies. Main prints after collection, so scheduling does not reorder the report. Queue capacity bounds queued jobs; it does not bound the already-loaded input vector’s total memory. A streaming input layer would need its own size and backpressure contract.
A plausible alternative: Start with a sequential reference and a clear input contract. Parallelize only after measurements show enough work to justify the coordination.

These representation choices make the required operations explicit and avoid accidental sign extension of char values. Unsigned modular addition is associative, so partial sums can be combined in any worker-completion order. A floating-point reduction or an order-sensitive hash would require a different argument. Choosing a simple additive checksum is what makes the parallel combination straightforward; it is not evidence of cryptographic strength.

slides.title: Virtual Memory → Process Isolation
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: All threads run inside one process and share its virtual address space.
Page permissions protect the process from unrelated private mappings, but they do not prevent one worker from accidentally indexing another slot incorrectly.
The queue carries validated slot indexes, and the program creates those indexes internally from a fixed bounded range.
No untrusted input becomes a pointer or slot identifier.
slides.narration:
All threads run inside one process and share its virtual address space. Page permissions protect the process from unrelated private mappings, but they do not prevent one worker from accidentally indexing another slot incorrectly. The queue carries validated slot indexes, and the program creates those indexes internally from a fixed bounded range. No untrusted input becomes a pointer or slot identifier. This shows how process isolation and object-level validation work together rather than substitute for one another.

In plain English: The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

slides.title: Processes → Files and I/O
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: The producer reads from standard input using the descriptor interface.
It checks the returned extent and publishes only the bytes actually obtained.
Input can come from a file or finite pipeline without changing the processing logic.
The example uses blocking input.
slides.narration:
The producer reads from standard input using the descriptor interface. It checks the returned extent and publishes only the bytes actually obtained. Input can come from a file or finite pipeline without changing the processing logic. The example uses blocking input. Queue closure cannot forcibly interrupt a producer already blocked in an external read. A production application needing responsive asynchronous cancellation would integrate readiness waiting and a cancellation event or use another explicitly cancellable I/O design. This limitation is part of the capstone’s stated scope.

In plain English: The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Queue push and pop operations use mutexes and condition variables.
The producer’s byte writes occur before publication into the ready queue; the worker’s successful dequeue establishes the visibility needed before reading those bytes.
The reverse handoff through the free queue ensures that the producer reuses a slot only after the previous worker has finished with it.
No extra atomic flag is needed per slot because the queue handoff supplies the ordering and exclusive ownership relationship.

keyPoints: Correct synchronization includes completion and failure.
Normal EOF closes the ready queue, allowing workers to drain and finish.

slides.title: A bounded concurrent byte-summary pipeline
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: The capstone imports the Chapter 49 queue rather than duplicating its synchronization implementation.
Eight slot indexes circulate through a free queue and a ready queue.
Each worker owns one private result element, combined only after joining.
Companion listing: ch61/pipeline.cpp
slides.narration:
The capstone imports the Chapter 49 queue rather than duplicating its synchronization implementation. Eight slot indexes circulate through a free queue and a ready queue. Each worker owns one private result element, combined only after joining. Companion listing: ch61/pipeline.cpp For ABC\n , the result is bytes=4 sum=208 workers=4 . For 100,000 generated bytes where byte i is i mod 256 , the result is bytes=100000 sum=12742320 workers=4 . The worker assignments can differ between runs while these totals remain fixed. The ownership invariant also explains why returning a slot to the free queue cannot block forever during normal completion. There are exactly eight slot identities. A worker holding one identity implies that at most seven others can already be in the free queue. The return therefore has room, assuming no identity was duplicated or lost. This is a progress proof derived from the resource model, not a timing assumption. On failure, no successful summary is printed. Some work may already have been processed, but the operation reports failure instead of presenting a partial aggregate as complete. The program does not implement a resumable checkpoint, input authentication, cryptographic hashing, or cancellation of a currently blocked external read. Those would be separate extensions with new contracts and tests.

In plain English: Imagine several people editing the same whiteboard. If they do not coordinate, the final answer can depend on who writes at exactly the wrong moment.

slides.title: Distinct output slots avoid a shared append operation
keyPoints: Allocate result storage before workers start
Assign each index once
Do not resize the vector while workers borrow its elements
Main reads and prints after completion
slides.narration: The workshop pipeline allocates the results vector before starting workers and assigns each work index once. Different workers can then write distinct result elements without competing to change container size. Having every worker call push_back on the same unprotected vector would instead race on shared container state and could invalidate storage. Main waits for completion before reading and printing, so report order follows input indexes rather than scheduling. The input strings are owned by work items, avoiding borrowed pointers into disappearing temporary data. These guarantees depend on the no-duplicate-index rule and the absence of concurrent resizing, not merely on choosing a vector type.

question.prompt: Why are writes to distinct pre-existing vector elements different from concurrent push_back calls?
question.answer: Distinct elements can be separate objects, while push_back modifies shared container bookkeeping and may reallocate storage. The fixed-storage and unique-index assumptions matter.

slides.title: Name the payload budget without claiming it covers everything
keyPoints: Eight 4096-byte slots provide 32 KiB of payload storage
Stacks, queues, metadata, and runtime state add more
A capacity-two work queue does not bound already-loaded input
slides.narration: The source streaming pipeline reuses eight four-kibibyte slots, giving thirty-two kibibytes of byte payload storage. That arithmetic excludes thread stacks, queue metadata, result objects, descriptors, and runtime overhead. It is not a claim that the entire process fits in one cache. The smaller workshop lab has a different boundary: its capacity-two queue bounds queued jobs, but the caller has already loaded the input vector of strings. Keeping these two implementations distinct prevents a false memory claim. To support large streaming input, the application must budget the producer's input ownership as well as the queue.

The queue's mutex and condition-variable protocol establishes the ordering that lets a worker safely read the filled data after a successful dequeue. The slot index is not just a number; it represents transfer of exclusive access. No extra per-slot atomic ready flag is needed in this design because the queue handoff supplies the synchronization. slides.title: The free queue publishes permission to reuse storage
keyPoints: Worker finishes all reads before returning the index
Producer cannot overwrite a worker-owned slot
Slot conservation also supports a progress argument
slides.narration: The reverse handoff matters as much as publication of filled data. A worker must finish reading the slot before returning its index to the free queue. Only after the producer obtains that index again may it overwrite the storage. In the eight-slot design, a worker holding one valid identity means at most seven other identities can already be in the free queue. Returning its identity therefore has room during normal completion, provided no slot was duplicated or lost. That is a resource-count argument for progress, not a guess that the producer will probably run soon.

slides.title: EOF closes production after publishing all valid bytes
keyPoints: A short positive read still contains useful input
Only the returned extent is published
Ready work drains before workers finish
slides.narration: A short read is not EOF. If the buffer can hold four thousand ninety-six bytes and read returns one hundred, the producer must publish those one hundred bytes with the slot's valid count. A later zero return ends input. Normal completion then closes the ready queue so workers can drain already-enqueued slots and stop once no work remains. The upstream pipe matters too: an accidentally retained write descriptor can prevent EOF even when no more bytes are intended. slides.title: Shutdown must wake waiters before collecting workers
keyPoints: Normal completion and failure have distinct paths
Failure closes queues so waiting threads can stop
Every created thread is joined before shared objects die
slides.narration: If a producer fails while workers wait on an empty ready queue, simply returning would leave blocked threads borrowing local queues and slots. The failure path records the error, closes the relevant queues, and joins every successfully created thread before destroying shared storage. Partial thread-creation failure needs the same care: earlier threads already exist even if a later creation throws. Scope ownership helps collect them, but a join cannot finish a worker that is waiting for an event nobody will send. Wakeup policy, error propagation, and lifetime order form one shutdown design.

slides.title: A stop hint does not publish unrelated shared data
keyPoints: The atomic failure flag only suggests stopping
Protected exception storage carries the actual error
Queue handoffs publish slots; joins complete worker results
slides.narration: The source uses different synchronization mechanisms for different facts. Its atomic failure flag is a stop hint, so relaxed ordering can be sufficient for that hint under the stated design. The actual exception object has protected storage, and thread joins govern completion before the caller accesses final state. Slot bytes become visible through queue handoffs, not through the relaxed flag. Mixing those roles is a common error: an atomic Boolean does not automatically publish every ordinary object nearby. slides.title: Closing a queue cannot interrupt every external wait
keyPoints: The producer uses blocking input in this capstone
Queue shutdown affects queue waiters
Responsive cancellation needs an explicit I/O wakeup design
slides.narration: The source deliberately accepts finite blocking input. If the producer is already blocked in read waiting for an external peer, closing an internal queue cannot force that read to return. blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Compute ranges from size and worker count instead of hardcoding groups of three, then test that ranges cover every index once. Preserve lifetime and disjoint result ownership while changing the partition rule. The extended lab uses this reasoning: Work items own their strings, so queue operations do not leave borrowed input pointers behind. Main assigns each index once; workers therefore write distinct result elements without resizing the vector. Queue predicates and close are protected by one mutex. Every normal and exceptional path closes the queue and collects workers before local shared state dies. Main prints after collection, so scheduling does not reorder the report. Queue capacity bounds queued jobs; it does not bound the already-loaded input vector’s total memory. A streaming input layer would need its own size and backpressure contract. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

slides.narration: The checksum does very little work per byte, so synchronization and scheduling overhead may exceed the benefit of several workers. Compare with the sequential utility on empty, tiny, boundary-sized, and larger finite binary fixtures. Keep output equality as a required condition, then measure the relevant timing boundary and CPU cost. Change slot size, slot count, or worker count one at a time when practical. A correct four-worker run is not automatically faster than one worker, and an impressive throughput number does not excuse excess memory or worse tail behavior in a different service context.

slides.narration: Finish by proposing one extension and defending its boundaries. A configurable worker count needs bounds and setup-failure cleanup. Larger inputs need a streaming ownership and memory budget. A stronger checksum needs an order-correct combination rule. A network input needs framing, deadlines, and cancellation beyond the internal queue. Keep the sequential reference and test empty input, exact slot boundaries, one byte beyond a boundary, binary nulls, and input errors.
